chapter_theme: Wealth does not stay with anyone: the feasting rich end up begging and kings lose their wives to enemies. Because death is near and certain, wealth should be shared and spent on virtue now, and the hoarder who neither enjoys nor gives has in effect already lost it.
structure_note: The quatrains move from examples of reversal (1-3) to the urgency created by death (4-7), then to the folly of the rich who forget it (8) and the hoarder's loss (9-10).

1.reading: Those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife, waving away a second helping, may go begging for gruel somewhere; so wealth is not a thing to be counted as lasting.
1.nuance: The detail of refusing the second mouthful sets the excess of the past against the single bowl of gruel begged later; the argument rests on a picture, not on a general claim.

2.reading: When blameless wealth comes, from that very day share its food with many, because wealth never stays level with anyone but turns like a cart wheel.
2.nuance: துகள்தீர் (blameless) qualifies the wealth to be shared: the verse assumes it was rightly gained. Mudaliar reads the food trodden out by beasts as a hint that others have a share in it.

3.reading: Even kings who rode in state on elephants under the royal umbrella, at the head of armies, fall and are changed when their deeds turn against them, and enemies take the wives they married.
3.nuance: Both commentators take ஏனை வினை as evil deeds that destroy; Pope keeps it as 'other deeds'. The verse itself names only 'the other deeds', so the cause of the fall is left in the vocabulary of karma rather than of war.

4.reading: Realise that the things you think will stand do not stand, and do what good you can at once, for your days are passing and Death is coming in anger.
4.nuance: Mudaliar notes that the first two doublings express abundance and the last two continuity: the form of the verse enacts days going and Death arriving.

5.reading: Whatever comes into your hand, do not hold it back thinking it can be given later; those who gave first will escape the waste land through which impartial Death drags his captives.
5.nuance: கோடில் makes Death impartial: it is the one force that does not favour the rich, which is why only what was given away counts.

6.reading: The appointed span of days cannot be exceeded and no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped; you who hold great wealth, give it away, for tomorrow the funeral drum may sound.
6.nuance: Mudaliar glosses the 'appointed day' as the lifespan set by past deeds, and cites Kural 269 for the verb குதித்தல், the very verb the verse uses to deny that anyone escapes.

7.reading: Using the sun as a measure, Death daily measures out and eats your days, so do much virtue and be compassionate; the closing line is read in more than one way.
7.nuance: The image makes each sunrise a scoop of grain taken from one's store of days. Pope reads the last line as 'none who are born escape death', which is a third reading beside the two commentators'.

positions.position: Whoever fails to do this, though born human, is counted among the unborn, that is, with beasts.
Be compassionate like the great who have reached the state of no further birth.
positions.quote: பிறவா நிலை யெய்திய பெரியோர் போல அருள் உடையவராகுக!

8.reading: The great wealth of the petty-minded, who say 'we are rich' and never think of where they must go, appears like lightning from a dark cloud at night and vanishes without a trace.
8.nuance: Both commentators take 'where they must go' as the next world, so the fault is not having wealth but forgetting the journey it cannot make.

9.reading: One who neither eats, nor wins honour, nor does deeds of renown, nor relieves the distress of close kin, nor gives, but only guards his wealth in vain, will be thought of with pity as one who has lost it.
9.nuance: The miser is pronounced to have lost his wealth while he still holds it: possession without use is already loss.

10.reading: Those who stint on clothing and food, wear down their bodies, do no lasting good and give nothing, will lose what they hoard, as the honey bee's store shows.
10.nuance: Mudaliar spells out the comparison: as someone else takes the honey the bees gathered, thieves and others take the hoard. The verse names only the bee as witness.

links.note: Both books make wealth's coming and going a spectacle: the Kural's crowd gathering and dispersing at a show, the Naladiyar's feaster turned beggar.
Both draw the same conclusion from wealth's instability: act on it at once (Kural 333) or share it from the day it comes (here).
The king on the elephant's neck under the royal umbrella appears in both. Here he falls when his deeds turn; in 21 he simply dies like everyone else.
Both urge good deeds before death stops them. The Kural pictures the hiccup that silences the tongue; this quatrain the angry approach of Death.
Both reject 'later': the Kural says virtue is the companion that does not perish when you do, and this quatrain says those who gave first escape Death's road.

Kural 269 says those with the power of austerity can leap past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்); this quatrain says no one here has leapt past Death and escaped. The conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's literal reading of 269; Kalaignar's figurative 'conquering death' softens it. Mudaliar cites 269 here.
Kural 331 calls taking the impermanent for permanent the lowest புல்லறிவு; this quatrain shows the புல்லறிவாளர் at it, with wealth that flashes and vanishes.
Both say that wealth neither enjoyed nor given is as good as none: in the Kural such a man has nothing, here he is thought to have lost it.
Both say wealth amassed by denying oneself (Kural தற்செற்று, here உடம்பு செற்றும்) and neglecting virtue goes to others. The Naladiyar adds the honey bee as witness.

source_issues: Shanmuganar's commentary throughout chapters 1-5 ends with a running number (61 for quatrain 1 to 110 for quatrain 50) and carries section headings numbered 8 to 12; the text matches the right quatrains, so the numbers seem to come from his edition.
Quatrain 6: the Tamil reads பிழைத்தெரிணஇக், apparently garbled; Mudaliar glosses ஒரீஇ, suggesting பிழைத்தொரீஇ. Mudaliar also glosses அகவா where the verse has இகவா.
Quatrain 10: the last word appears as கா஢ with a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss கரி (witness) gives the reading.
Quatrain 10: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
